What Makes Technology “Civic”?

A1 — Civic Technology Analysis · Week 1 · Pietro Chiri · 11.458 Crowd Sourced City – Civic Tech Prototyping · Assignment 1 · Monday, September 14, 2026

Civil society has completely fallen out of love with the promise of a better future. The average American citizen is closer to bankruptcy than to ever becoming a millionaire, let alone a billionaire. The promise of the American dream has deflated completely, as homeownership, universal healthcare, accessible high education, and fair grocery prices seem impossible to obtain in the near future. In fact, a recent New York Times article compiles the opinions of several ten-year-olds interviewed on what life is going to be like by the year 2050. The answers are far from encouraging: bigger wealth gap, increasing cost of living, sparking wars, surviving rather than living. The political, economic, and moral crises of our current times call for meaningful action if we’re ever going to pull ourselves out of the post-pandemic tipping point onto the next quarter century.

Under these bleak circumstances, the authors of Power to the Public: The Promise of Public Interest Technology (2021) state the following: “There is no solving the world’s hardest problems without governments and institutions that really work for people”. And there lies the main issue: civil society has lost trust in their own democratic leaders who, originally meant to serve them, have rather pushed the middle class downwards while lobbying for their own financial interests. The authors Dawson McGuinness and Schank, however, decide to take a more optimistic approach in their set of core principles:

“Although … governments have failed, we believe deeply in government and the people who work in government at all levels. Government workers are not the problem. Government is not the problem. The problems lie in the systems, incentives, and structures government inhabits, which are no longer aligned well with serving its citizenry in a digital era.” (Preface p. xiv)

Whichever way technology is meant to serve communities at different scales, initiatives and techniques that promote the public good are certainly not new, dating far back the digital age (now the fast-pacing AI age). In Chapter 5, titled “How We Got Here and Where We’re Going,” the authors differentiate terminology for tools that essentially aim for governments to approach problem solving. Terms like “public interest technology,” “civic tech,” or “gov tech” are related phrases that practitioners may use indiscriminately, yet sprung in different historical times and may have responded to different needs.

On the one hand, “public interest technology” is defined by the authors as “the application of design, data, and delivery to advance the public interest and promote the public good in the digital age” (See Image 1). The term originates from law practice in the 1970s, when funders like the Ford Foundation saw a need for law school graduates to serve the public and fill in positions in the public sector. Likewise, a stronger public sector meant incorporating the innovative know-how of the private sector: effective use of technology based on data collection and analysis, high capacity to test and improve a minimum viable product, among others. Public interest technology builds on the notion of open government and open data, so that a government’s actions is available to everyone.

Terms like “civic tech,” on the other hand, overlaps and helps build the new field of public interest technology. Instead of heavily relying on cutting-edge technology (such as machine learning algorithms, cloud-based tools, etc.), public interest technology refers to the methodology that, though still technology-dependent, focuses more on the end users and progress tracking. The historical use of said terms also comes into play. Civic tech aimed to bring transparency and technology to governments as an early movement in the 1980s and 1990s, drawing from nonprofits organizations such as Computer Professionals for Social Responsibility and the Electronic Frontier Foundation. However, the new millennium and the democratization of internet access led to new ways in which an open government could be more transparent. Under the Obama administration, the 2009 Open Government Directive allowed for information to be publicly available online. As the authors state, open data at its core allows citizens to hold governments accountable in the digital age.

A recent encounter of mine with a public interest technology was during my summer internship with Slum Dwellers International in Cape Town, South Africa. SDI focuses on informal settlement upgrading across a network of 20+ countries in the Global South, with women and youth at the forefront of driving long-lasting change in their communities through data collection processes and negotiations with local governments. Recently, as part of the SDI Impact Innovation initiative, the Decision Labs consultancy is developing and operationalizing the City Data Platform for 7 pilot cities, as well as a cross-city dashboard (See Image 2). The platform aims to compile spatial quantitative and qualitative data on informal settlements in seven pilot cities in Africa. During part of my internship, I supported this taskforce with a user persona analysis. The purpose of the user persona analysis was to provide Decision Labs with insights into users’ needs, wants, and overall considerations, which have implications for the platform’s backend (data lake), the frontend (dashboard). The end users were the community members, the municipal officers, researchers in academia, and the SDI Network secretariat. Though it’s still a work in progress, I truly enjoyed the way the nonprofit organization was primarily thinking about the end users and the established synergy between community-collected data and novel technologies.

Sources

Tara Dawson McGuinness & Hana Schank, Power to the Public: The Promise of Public Interest Technology (Princeton University Press, 2021) – Preface & Chapter 5

VII. Notes

Short uncertainty/interpretation note identifying at least one issue that was not simply a number copied from a table.

  • LOT – The main issue I encountered while working with this parcel was its extremely irregular shape, instead of the traditional, easy-to-work-with, rectangular-shaped lot. The L-shaped parcel with pronounced angles made it difficult to understand how the setbacks work, especially that of the rear yard.
  • SETBACK-DEFINED BUILDABLE AREA – Therefore, to obtain a setback-defined width, I didn’t use neither the left measurement nor the right measurement, but rather an approximated depth calculated as Lot Area ÷ Frontage.
  • BUILDING FOOTPRINT – The inner gray trapezoidal-shaped building footprint is calculated based on the 30% lot coverage requirement. Similar to the setback-defined buildable area, the shape and angles for the building footprint seemed highly irregular to work with.

From Zoning to Civic Technology – An ADU Comparative Analysis

A3 — Zoning Consequences · Week 3 · Pietro Chiri · 11.458 Crowd Sourced City – Civic Tech Prototyping · Assignment 3 · Monday, September 28, 2026

I. Compare Massachusetts and Boston ADU Regulations

Identify several important similarities and differences between the Massachusetts statewide ADU framework and Boston's approach.

The ADU frameworks for both the state of Massachusetts and the city of Boston share the basic common understanding of what an Accessory Dwelling Unit is. Both define an ADU as a self-contained unit with its own entrance, kitchen, and bathroom within the same lot as a main residence. Both recognize the same three types: internal, attached, and detached. Both treat ADUs as an opportunity for families to house their elderly or young relatives, or even earn an extra rental income. Both as constrained by the Fire Safety Code (NFPA), which may require additional sprinklers or other equipment.

However, the key difference between the Massachusetts statewide ADU framework and the Boston ADU regulations is that the state law does not apply to the city of Boston. The state passed the Affordable Homes Act, which created as-of-right ADUs in single-family zoning districts. Every municipality in the state of Massachusetts, with the single exception of Boston, derives its updated ADU zoning codes from the state’s. Boston’s autonomy on drafting its own ADU ordinance has led to more detailed considerations regarding permitted square footage and as-of-right permitting.

Square Footage

On the one hand, the MAPC ADU law requires that ADUs of up to 900 square feet must be allowed. There is, however, certain flexibility. Gwendolyn Hellen-Sands, Senior Regional Housing and Land Use Planner at the MAPC, explained that “municipalities may define Protected Use ADUs as larger than 900sf or larger than 50% the GFA of the primary dwelling unit.” For Boston, the maximum size is more specifically tailored to Mattapan neighborhood: “By right only in Mattapan R1/R2: building floor plate up to 900 sq ft or the floor plate of the main house, whichever is less (Article 60). Elsewhere the code has no detached-ADU rule, so any size needs a ZBA variance.”

Moreover, the Boston ADU Guidebook shows an example of the medium-sized lot with an attached ADU on the corner lot with a gross square footage of 1350sf. These variances in more constrained or more generous ADU areas are important to consider.

II. What Makes These Rules Difficult to Navigate?

Drawing on the course readings and class discussions, identify 2–3 significant challenges that someone might encounter when trying to translate these regulations into a real project.

As-of-right

During the second LCAU “Decoding/Encoding” session, Will Cohen (Senior Planner in the City of Boston Planning Department), pointed out an ironic incongruity: Boston did not have a regulatory zoning act until 1924, and over 60% of the buildings in the city predate 1924. Thus, with an institutionalized set of bureaucratic barriers, zoning code protects changes to Boston neighborhoods from happening, rather than facilitating construction of new buildings. As a matter of fact, most of the pre-1924 buildings could not be developed today as-of-right, precisely because they wouldn’t be compliant with the current zoning. For instance, Cohen exemplifies with how 99% of the current residential lots in West Roxbury, Hyde Park, and Roslindale are non-conforming to zoning code.

The inadvertent consequence is a housing affordability crisis. According to Gray in “Arbitrary Lines,” there’s a close relationship between zoning and high housing costs. Not only does the current zoning code block housing construction that could respond to the increasing demand, but also the bureaucratic permitting process poses another yet layer of housing inaccessibility. Gray argues that “zoning today throws many developments out of this as-of-right process and into a prolonged, expensive, and unpredictable show permitting process.” (2022: p. 61)

Mattapan sits as an interesting case study among these discussions. In December 2024, the ADU Guidebook was released, and ever since, Mattapan adopted this new zoning reform that grants homeowners more flexibility on building ADUs, having rezoned over 3600 parcels and 130 blocks. However, in two years since, only 10 existing homes have added ADUs as-of-right. The number is disappointingly small given the incredible work the Planning Department has done on proposing zoning reforms. The small advancements in implementation and delivery is still an issue to navigate and overcome.

Price

Moreover, ADUs are tremendously expensive. Gwendolyn Hellen-Sands from MAPC admits that the minimum cost is usually around $200k, while Will Cohen alerts how building and fire code regulations can add excessive costs to a seemingly simple project. Sprinkler requirements, extra HVAC, new plumbing, and a long etcetera make ADUs financially not feasible for many households. This creates a fundamental mismatch between the promise of ADUs as an affordable housing solution and the financial reality of building one. As a result, zoning reform alone may not be enough to meaningfully expand ADU production. On top of that, Cohen even clearly stated that ADUs will not solve the housing problem in Boston even if every available lot could smoothly implement one.

III. What Could a Tool Actually Help With?

Based on your analysis, identify one or more specific problems that a digital tool could realistically help solve.

Based on the previous responses and analysis, a handful of ideas for a public interest tech-driven tool come to mind. For this section, I have come up with three functions that the tool we develop throughout the remaining of the course could have. For each feature, I’m considering who the user persona is, which question/concern does the feature tackle, and a bit more explanation:

Option 1: The ADU Roadmap

  • User: homeowner.
  • Question: "What rules even apply to my lot?"
  • Someone in Salem and someone in Mattapan may face different legal frameworks for ADUs, let alone the fact that most day-to-day people may not know that Boston is exempt from the state law. This tool feature would take an address and show key information: jurisdiction (state framework vs. Boston), zoning district, zoning overlays, parks buffer, flood zones, among others. Internally, the app follows a decision tree to recommend a specific pathway (i.e. "internal ADU by-right," or “detached ADU with new sprinkler system”). These pathway results should be accompanied by illustrations that provide the homeowner with a clear visual idea of what can be done.

Option 2: The ADU Feasibility Calculator

  • User: homeowner.
  • Question: "Is an ADU financially realistic for me?”
  • If the project costs over $200k or more, the legal permit to build now becomes the least of the homeowner’s worries. The tool would compare internal, attached, and detached options and flags what is bearing the extra costs (i.e. sprinkler requirements). The tool shows cost ranges (not a quotes, since it’s not making financing recommendations). The tool could also serve as a general contractor “middleman” that, by providing essential information on what can and cannot be built, essentially unburdens the homeowner with unnecessary costs. Drawing from the r/Massachusetts and r/AccessoryDwelllings subreddits, cutting out the middleman fee could potentially save the client tens of thousands of dollars.

Option 3: A Drop-off Diagnostic

  • User: City of Boston and MAPC
  • Question: "Why did rezoning 3,600 parcels in Mattapan produce only about 10 ADUs?"
  • Going to the trouble of reforming zoning regulations should reflect in a positive outcome of hundreds if not thousands of new ADUs. However, that has not been the case throughout Boston nor across the state. This tool feature would ask residents who started the process where did they stopped (cost, design, financing, confusion, lot constraints). This would allow for a better diagnostic of what is going wrong, and could tell the client where the real bottleneck is.

IV. What Would We Need to Build It?

Identify what we would need to know, collect, structure, or build in order to make your proposed tool possible.

Making any of these tools possible starts with identifying what already exists. A good deal of material is already public: Boston's zoning text (including Article 60 for Mattapan), the state's ADU framework, and Boston ADU Guidebook. Parcel, building footprint, and assessing data are available through Analyze Boston, and GIS layers from MassGIS and FEMA cover flood zones, open space, and other overlays. The city's building permit records could also show where ADUs have actually been approved. However, almost none of this is structured in a way a tool can use. The zoning text would have to be translated into machine-readable rules: a dimensional requirements table covering setbacks, lot coverage, height, and maximum floor plate. This data-analysis task would then feed a decision tree that turns a parcel's characteristics into a recommended pathway, like "internal ADU by-right" or "detached ADU requiring a variance." (Option 1)

Moreover, some quantitative and qualitative information does not exist in any dataset and would have to come from the users themselves: conditions of the existing house, household budget, etc. We have no clear itemized construction cost data of an ADU, especially for the Fire code elements that make the cost skyrocket. Based on what I have learned so far, I recommend that our class focus on one well-defined problem: why eligible parcels in Mattapan are not becoming ADUs. (Option 3) The city rezoned over 3,600 parcels, yet only about 10 homes have added an ADU as-of-right. This is the clearest, most measurable gap between regulation and delivery we have found! A parcel-level eligibility and pathway check limited to Mattapan's R1/R2 districts is achievable with data that already exists. It can also double as a research tool: by asking users where they would stop and why, it would give the City and MAPC evidence about whether the bottleneck is confusion, cost, financing, or lot constraints. That evidence is exactly what we need prior to starting the ADU Feasibility calculator. (Option 2)
